sources.news_title: Venezuela’s Other Hunger Entrepreneur Falls Into the Hands of the United States
sources.text:
El otro empresario del hambre de Venezuela cae en manos de Estados Unidos
Álvaro Pulido es acusado de haber cometido fraude por valor de más de 2.000 millones de dólares y era un estrecho socio de Alex Saab, el testaferro de Nicolás Maduro
Corresponsal en Washington
La colaboración de las autoridades que gobiernan Venezuela con Washington de supervisor alcanza ya de lleno a los empresarios que durante años hicieron fortuna al amparo del chavismo. Primero fue Alex Saab, indultado por Joe Biden y devuelto este año a Estados Unidos por ... el régimen de Delcy Rodríguez. Ahora, por sorpresa, es su socio, Álvaro Pulido, el otro empresario del hambre venezolano, según se le apodó en la primera Administración Trump. El fiscal general estadounidense, Todd Blanche, anunció este domingo, 11 de octubre, su extradición. Le esperan dos causas federales, trece cargos y acusaciones sobre operaciones que movieron casi 2.000 millones de dólares.
Pulido estaba preso en Venezuela. Agentes de la DEA lo sacaron de una cárcel venezolana para trasladarlo a Florida. Esa salida apunta a la cooperación de Caracas, aunque las autoridades estadounidenses no han detallado públicamente cómo se ejecutó. La portavoz de la fiscalía norteamericana Nicole Navas Oxman confirmó su custodia y anunció que comparecerá el martes ante un tribunal de Miami.
Blanche presentó la detención como un golpe a los negocios ligados al régimen de Nicolás Maduro. En su anuncio acusó a Pulido de corromper programas destinados a proporcionar alimentos, medicinas y viviendas para enriquecerse, utilizando además el sistema financiero estadounidense. El mensaje del fiscal general incluía una advertencia: dijo que ni el tiempo transcurrido ni la distancia impedirían perseguir a los responsables y llevarlos ante un tribunal norteamericano.
Noticia relacionada
En el primer expediente, presentado en julio de 2019 contra Pulido y Saab, la fiscalía describe una operación sencilla y rentable: cobrar varias veces por una misma importación. Los empresarios habían obtenido un contrato para construir viviendas sociales. Según los investigadores, presentaban facturas y documentos falsos para conseguir dólares del sistema venezolano de control de cambios.
Un cargamento podía convertirse, sobre el papel, en varios. Los funcionarios sonornados fotografiaban los mismos materiales de construcción en lugares diferentes para aparentar nuevas entregas. Después se solicitaban nuevos pagos. Para mantener el mecanismo, la trama habría sobornado a empleados de aduanas, de la Guardia Nacional Bolivariana y de Cadivi, el organismo encargado de administrar las divisas.
La acusación cifra en exactamente 350.041.500 dólares las transferencias realizadas desde cuentas venezolanas, a través de bancos estadounidenses, hacia cuentas extranjeras controladas por los socios. Ese expediente contiene ocho cargos contra Pulido: uno de conspiración para blanquear dinero y siete de blanqueo. Esa es la causa en la que Joe Biden indultó a Saab en 2023, pero ahora Pulido rendirá cuentas por ella.
Sobornos en comida y salud
La segunda causa, presentada en octubre de 2021, entra directamente en el negocio de la comida y los medicamentos, de ahí la referencia al hambre de los venezolanos. Los fiscales sostienen que Pulido y sus colaboradores conseguían contratos mediante sobornos, elevaban los precios y distribuían el dinero entre empresarios, intermediarios y funcionarios. Las necesidades básicas de los venezolanos se convertían así, según la acusación, en una fuente de beneficios privados.
Se vendieron diez millones de cajas de alimentos a 34 dólares cada una, por un total de 340 millones. El escrito sostiene que el entonces gobernador de Táchira, José Gregorio Vielma Mora, conocía que producirlas e importarlas costaba considerablemente menos. La diferencia permitía pagar sobornos y repartir ganancias. Otro contrato de alimentos ascendía a 369,9 millones; dos de medicamentos sumaban cerca de 146 millones.
En este auto aparecen también el hijo de Pulido, Emmanuel Enrique Rubio González, y otros integrantes de la red. Se atribuyen a Pulido cinco cargos adicionales. La petición de decomiso asciende a 1.607 millones de dólares. Cada uno de los trece cargos de ambas causas contempla hasta veinte años de prisión, aunque las penas no se suman automáticamente.
🚨 Law enforcement on the @HSTaskForce arrested Alvaro Pulido Vargas where he now faces two separate federal indictments in the U.S. from 2019 and 2021 involving an alleged multibillion-dollar Venezuelan money laundering and bribery schemes tied to the Maduro regime. His alleged actions show a blatant disregard to the Venezuelan people by corrupting government programs intended to provide critical food, medicine, and housing for personal enrichment and exploiting the American financial system to do it. No amount of time or distance will stop @TheJusticeDept from working with our federal law enforcement and international partners to pursue these criminals and bring them to justice in an American courtroom.
— Attorney General Todd Blanche (@AGToddBlanche) October 11, 2026
El regreso de Saab a Estados Unidos anticipó este desenlace. Biden lo había indultado el 20 de diciembre de 2023, dentro de un intercambio de prisioneros con Venezuela. Pero aquel perdón estaba limitado al caso de 2019: no cerraba la puerta a perseguir otros delitos. El 16 de mayo de 2026, las autoridades venezolanas anunciaron su deportación. El empresario que Maduro había defendido y hasta hecho ministro quedó nuevamente al alcance de la justicia estadounidense.
Esta vez, Saab terminó admitiendo su responsabilidad. El 15 de septiembre se declaró culpable de conspiración para blanquear dinero en una nueva causa sobre contratos de alimentos y medicamentos. Reconoció haber organizado pagos ilegales para conseguir adjudicaciones públicas. Afronta hasta veinte años de prisión.

sources.news_title: Businessman Wanted in Venezuela Bribery Case Now in U.S. Custody
sources.text:
Alvaro Pulido was indicted in federal court in Miami in 2019 and again in 2021 during an investigation into his longtime business associate, Alex Saab, a former ally of ousted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration and State Department had offered a reward of up to $10 million for information leading to Pulido’s arrest.
Pulido’s detention followed an investigation involving the DEA, FBI and Homeland Security Investigations, Nicole Navas Oxman, a spokesperson for the Homeland Security Task Force, said Sunday.
Oxman did not disclose how Pulido came into U.S. custody. She said, however, that he is scheduled to make his initial court appearance in Miami on Tuesday.
Venezuelan authorities have not publicly commented on the arrest. The silence underscores the difficult political position facing acting President Delcy Rodríguez as she seeks to placate members of the ruling coalition who oppose efforts by the Trump administration to pursue Venezuelan insiders wanted in the United States, in some cases for years, on serious charges including corruption and drug trafficking.
Pulido, who was born in Colombia, was arrested in Venezuela in 2023 as part of a sweeping corruption investigation at the state-run oil company PDVSA. Rodríguez led that crackdown while serving as Maduro’s vice president. She became Venezuela’s acting president after U.S. forces ousted Maduro in January.
DON’T MISS: BBC Faces Talent Exodus Warning After Top Presenter Quits
U.S. prosecutors allege that Pulido and Saab built a network of offshore shell companies to route bribe payments to senior Maduro allies. In return, the pair allegedly secured government contracts to import food, medicine and affordable housing during a period of severe hardship across Venezuela.
Saab, who is also from Colombia, was deported to the United States by Rodríguez in May. He pleaded guilty last month in a related bribery case and agreed to cooperate with U.S. investigators pursuing Maduro and others. As part of the agreement, Saab will forfeit $195 million in criminal proceeds linked to the corruption scheme.

sources.news_title: Businessman wanted for years for allegedly bribing Venezuelan officials finally in U.S. custody
sources.text:
Businessman wanted for years for allegedly bribing Venezuelan officials finally in U.S. custody
A businessman wanted for years in the U.S. for allegedly paying bribes to top Venezuelan officials in exchange for lucrative state contracts in Venezuela has been taken into custody.
Alvaro Pulido was indicted in Miami federal court in 2019 and again in 2021 as part of an investigation into his longtime business partner, Alex Saab, a one-time ally of ousted President Nicolás Maduro. The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration and State Department had been offering a reward of up to $10 million for information leading to his arrest.
Pulido was taken into U.S. custody after an investigation led by the DEA, FBI and Homeland Security Investigations agencies, Nicole Navas Oxman, a Homeland Security Task Force spokesperson, said Sunday.
Oxman didn't say how Pulido ended up in U.S. custody but said he will make his initial court appearance Tuesday in Miami.
Venezuelan authorities have so far been silent about the arrest, reflecting the challenge acting President Delcy Rodríguez faces in appeasing elements of the ruling coalition that want her to resist attempts by the Trump administration to round up scores of Venezuelan insiders wanted by the U.S., sometimes for years, for serious crimes ranging from corruption to drug trafficking.
The Colombian-born Pulido was arrested in Venezuela in 2023 as part of a sprawling crackdown on corruption inside state-run oil company PDVSA that was led by Rodríguez while she was serving as Maduro's vice president. She took over as Venezuela's acting president following the U.S. military's ouster of Maduro in January.
Prosecutors allege that Pulido, together with Saab, created a network of offshore shell companies to funnel bribes to top Maduro allies in exchange for contracts to import food, medicine and low-cost housing at a time of widespread hardship in the South American country.
Saab, who also hails from Colombia, was deported to the U.S. by Rodríguez in May. Last month, he pleaded guilty in a related bribery case, agreeing to cooperate against Maduro and other individuals and forfeit $195 million in criminal proceeds from the corruption scheme.

sources.text:
Alvaro Pulido is a former Venezuelan businessman. He was indicted on bribery charges in the United States in 2019 and in 2021 as part of a larger investigation into a business partner.
Now, Alvaro Pulido is in an American cell, awaiting trial. He will be appearing this week in a Miami court.

That last part is the fun part; it's not clear if Pulido was already in the United States and was arrested here, or if he was somehow, shall we say, transported here involuntarily by parties as yet unknown. That is what happened to his former business partner's "ally" Nicolás Maduro, after all.
Saab and Pulido are accused of setting up and operating a chain of shell companies with which to shovel bribe money at Maduro and some of his top allies, in exchange for lucrative import contracts for things like food and medicines. Saab was deported to the United States in May, by Venezuela's interim president Delcy Rodríguez; he has since pleaded guilty in another, related case.
Here's the really telling piece of the report:
Venezuelan authorities have so far been silent about the arrest, reflecting the challenge acting President Delcy Rodríguez faces appeasing elements of the ruling coalition that want her to resist attempts by the Trump administration to round up scores of Venezuelan insiders wanted by the U.S., sometimes for years, for serious crimes ranging from corruption to drug trafficking.
Ay, that's the rub. Delcy Rodríguez isn't sailing on smooth, blue and serene waters in Venezuela. She is a place-holder, marking time until the country has its next elections in 2027. If Venezuela's elections are honest, she will likely find herself standing in whatever passes for an unemployment line once the votes are tallied. But she is a Maduro creature, having served as his vice president, and it's a certainty that there are still elements in Venezuela, in and out of government, who stand to gain from keeping what's left of the Maduro regime in power.
Venezuela should be on its way to being a wealthy, prosperous modern nation, if for no other reason than that they are sitting atop the world's largest known oil reserves. But Venezuela has been a country where bribery schemes like this were an expected way of doing business, and that kind of culture is hard to shake off, even if you have the steely eyes of the United States on your doings.
Things should stabilize some after the elections, but those are some ways off yet.

By Joshua Goodman And Alanna Durkin Richer The Associated Press
MIAMI (AP) — A businessman wanted for years in the U.S. for allegedly paying bribes to top Venezuelan officials in exchange for lucrative state contracts in Venezuela has been taken into custody, American authorities said on Sunday.
Alvaro Pulido was indicted in Miami federal court in 2019 and again in 2021 as part of an investigation into his longtime business partner, Alex Saab, a one-time ally of ousted President Nicolás Maduro. The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration and the State Department had been offering a reward of up to $10 million for information leading to his arrest.
Pulido was taken into U.S. custody after an investigation led by the DEA, FBI and Homeland Security Investigations agencies, said Nicole Navas Oxman, a Homeland Security Task Force spokesperson.
